name: Crucible Weld & Fab Supervisory Jacket
description:
Crucible's floor supervisors wear this jacket as a mark of rank that separates them from the standard-issue maintenance jumpsuits of the line workers below them. Constructed from a flame-resistant aramid-cotton blend with a reflective Crucible anvil logo across the back in heat-resistant silver ink, the jacket is rated for incidental weld splash and short-duration heat exposure up to 400°C. The sleeves roll and secure at the elbow for close-quarters work, and the chest carries a row of magnetic tool clips that hold diagnostic tablets, torque drivers, and site-communication hardware. Color is Crucible's signature industrial orange over a graphite underlayer.

The jacket is built wide at the shoulders to fit the range of body types that come up through Crucible's apprenticeship tracks, including workers with significant upper-body chrome — reinforced seams at the shoulder accommodate most cybernetic arm attachment points, and the back panel is cut to allow tail-loop access for geneware-modified supervisors. It's not glamorous work wear, but it's built to last: most supervisors wear the same jacket for 5–8 years before it needs replacement, and the culture around Crucible sites means a battered jacket is a sign of experience, not neglect.
cultural_context: On a Crucible site, the orange jacket is authority. Line workers know it, and Crucible site managers know that the jacket does half their management work for them. Workers who get promoted to supervisor sometimes feel the weight of putting it on for the first time — it changes how people look at you, and not always in ways you expected.
story_hooks: A supervisor's jacket is found at a site where an industrial 'accident' killed three line workers. The jacket's tool clips still hold a diagnostic tablet with data someone wanted buried.
A longtime supervisor is quietly demoted and stripped of his orange jacket — the official reason is performance, but he knows it's because he filed a safety complaint.
Someone is counterfeiting Crucible supervisor jackets and using them to walk unchallenged through restricted manufacturing zones.

physical_description.visual_profile: A broad-shouldered work jacket in high-visibility industrial orange with graphite grey underlayer visible at cuffs and collar. The back features a large reflective silver anvil logo—Crucible's mark of authority. Despite its utilitarian construction, it reads as confident and command-oriented on the wearer; the silhouette suggests capability and experience rather than fashion.
physical_description.fit: Generously cut through the shoulders and torso to accommodate diverse body types and upper-body augmentation. Sleeves are slightly relaxed but taper toward rollable cuffs secured at the elbow. The cut allows freedom of movement without excess fabric—practical for close-quarters fabrication work.
physical_description.primary_material: Flame-resistant aramid-cotton blend rated for 400°C incidental exposure and weld splash. Durable, slightly stiff when new, softening with wear. Graphite grey visible at seams and interior.
physical_description.texture: Structured, with a subtle ribbed weave. Reinforced seams throughout, especially at shoulders. The reflective anvil logo has a raised, heat-resistant quality. Shows scuff marks and minor discoloration easily, patina deepening with use.
physical_description.color_scheme: Crucible industrial orange (primary) over graphite grey. Heat-resistant silver reflective ink on back logo. No bright accent colors—pure function.
physical_description.closures: Heavy-duty magnetic snaps down the front placket. Magnetic tool clips along the chest in a deliberate row—form following function. Cuff closures at elbows via friction-fit retention straps.
distinctive_features: Large reflective silver anvil logo centered on back panel
Row of magnetic tool clips on chest for diagnostic tablets and hardware
Reinforced shoulder seams to accommodate cybernetic arm attachment points
Tail-loop access cut into back panel for geneware modifications
Roll-and-secure sleeves at elbow for precision work
Visible wear patterns become badges of experience—scuff marks, fading, heat discoloration accepted as proof of tenure
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2-3 functional authority wear. Not wealthy, but clearly positioned above line workers. Signals mid-management access and earned competence.
physical_description.cultural_context: Uniform of a Crucible floor supervisor in the GLMZ manufacturing sector. Wearing this jacket means you've proven yourself on the line and earned the trust of site management. It carries social weight—workers defer, managers listen. A battered jacket is a resume of survival and expertise. The fit accommodates the mixed-augmentation reality of Crucible's workforce without comment.
physical_description.condition_typical: Worn in deliberately. New jackets look slightly stiff and overly bright; veteran jackets show heat scars, minor burns, chemical stains, and discoloration that supervisors wear like medals. A pristine jacket signals either a recent promotion or someone still proving themselves.

image_prompt: Industrial-grade work jacket in burnt orange and graphite grey on a weathered neo-noir worker, sleeves rolled at elbows. Large reflective silver anvil logo visible on back. Close-up detail of magnetic tool clips holding diagnostic hardware on chest. Harsh warehouse lighting casting long shadows, grime and heat-scars visible on fabric. Dark metallic factory backdrop with hanging cables and industrial fixtures. Moody, utilitarian aesthetic. --ar 2:3 --v 6
